verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! For good [is] singing-praise [to] our God, for pleasant, [for] fitting [is] praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Lift up your voices to Yah. How good it is to sing to our God, how sweet, how fitting, how right that praise should rise.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens as the whole last section of the Psalter does, with the plural command hallelu-Yah, 'praise Yah': an order to a crowd, not a private sigh. Yah is the short form of the divine name, and the command has the sound of a shout that a choir takes up. The three adjectives that follow (good, pleasant, fitting) are not decoration. Tov is 'good' in the moral and practical sense, na'im is 'pleasant' to the ear and the heart, and na'avah is 'fitting, becoming', the word used of a garment that suits its wearer. The KJV 'comely' is archaic but accurate, though it hides that the same word is used in Psalm 33:1 for praise suited to the upright (Metzudat Zion cites that verse). Zamerah is an infinitive, 'singing', and zamar is the root for praise sung with instruments, which prepares the harp in verse 7. Note that the KJV adds 'it is' three times (in italics in the old Bibles) because the Hebrew has no verb: the lines are fragments of delight. Ibn Ezra and Meiri hear in the whole psalm a hymn of redemption and return from exile, and the next verse bears them out.

philological_notes.note: A verbal noun (infinitive) of zamar, 'to make music, to sing to the accompaniment of an instrument'; the final he is a form of the infinitive, not a feminine noun. 'Good is singing to our God.'
'Fitting, becoming, beautiful'; the same word describes praise in Psalm 33:1. Praise suits God as a robe suits a king.

verses.translation_literal: Builder of Jerusalem [is] YHWH; the driven-away of Israel he gathers.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is the one who builds Jerusalem. The scattered of Israel, the ones driven out, he draws in again, one by one, until they are home.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the reason for praise is given, and it begins with the participle 'builder', placed first for emphasis: not 'the LORD builds' but 'Builder of Jerusalem, the LORD'. A participle describes what he is doing, not a single act of the past, so the verse sounds like news that is still unfolding. The setting is almost certainly the return from Babylon and the rebuilding of the city's walls (compare Nehemiah 12), and the tradition took it as promise too: Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read 'he will build'. Nidchei is the passive participle of nadach, 'to thrust away, banish', and the KJV 'outcasts' is a fair rendering, though the BBE 'outlaws' is wrong: these people were not criminals but the driven. The verb yekhannes, 'he gathers', is the verb Esther uses to call the Jews of Susa together (Ibn Ezra cites 'go, gather all the Jews'). Notice the symmetry: the city and its people are built and gathered at once, as if the wall and the exiles were two halves of the same house.

philological_notes.note: Passive participle of nadach, 'to be thrust away, driven off', here 'the driven-away [ones] of'; not 'outlaws' as the BBE has it.

verses.translation_literal: The healer of the broken of heart and binder-up of their pains.
verses.translation_dramatic: He heals the ones whose hearts are broken. He binds up their pain as a hand wraps a wound, slowly, with care.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse has no finite verb: two participles hang in the air, 'the healer', 'the binder', so it sounds like a title spoken with tenderness. In Hebrew thought the heart (lev) is the seat of mind and will as much as of feeling, so 'broken of heart' means a person whose resolve, hope and spirit have been shattered, as the exiles were (Radak: 'Israel, who are broken of heart and grieved in exile'). The image of binding is medical: chavash is to wrap a wound with a bandage, as in Ezekiel 34:4, where the shepherds failed to bind up the injured sheep (Metzudat Zion cites that verse). The KJV 'wounds' for 'atzevot is a gamble: the word comes from the root 'tz-v, 'to hurt, to grieve', and means pains or griefs, as the YLT has it. Here God does not just comfort; he is a physician, and the same writer who counts stars next is the one who bends over a wound. The BBE adds 'oil', which the Hebrew does not have.

philological_notes.note: From 'tz-v, 'to hurt, grieve'. Here 'their pains' or 'griefs'; 'wounds' (KJV) is an inference from the verb 'bind up', and Ibn Ezra reads it as the injuries felt by those touched by great sorrow.
To bind or wrap, as a bandage, or a turban; used of binding wounds in Ezekiel 34:4.

verses.translation_literal: Counter of a number for the stars; to all of them names he calls.
verses.translation_dramatic: He counts the stars, every one. And to each of them, by name, he speaks.
verses.directors_commentary: The camera lifts from the wound to the night sky. The point is a contrast of scale: the one who bends over a single broken heart is the one who counts the stars, which no human can do (God told Abraham to try in Genesis 15:5, as Radak and Meiri note). In the ancient Near East the stars were gods or the agents of gods, and Babylon's priests mapped and named them to read fate; here they are objects in a roll call, each counted and each named by the God of Israel, so they have no independence and no say over anyone's fortune. Malbim hears an explicit polemic against rule by the stars. Naming in Hebrew is an act of authority: whoever names owns and commands. The KJV 'telleth' is archaic for 'counts' (to tell a sheep is to count it), and the modern reader hears 'tell' as 'speak', which loses the arithmetic. Note the two verbs of the participle: moneh (count) and yiqra' (calls), the second a finite imperfect, as if he is calling now.

philological_notes.note: 'Counting, assigning'; the KJV 'telleth' means 'counts', as in 'tell the tale of bricks'. A participle, so the counting is ongoing.
Calling names is a sign of authority over what is named; the stars are summoned like a roll call. Compare Isaiah 40:26, which Radak quotes alongside this verse.

verses.translation_literal: Great [is] our Lord and abundant of power; to his understanding there is no number.
verses.translation_dramatic: Great is our Lord, vast in strength. And his understanding? There is no counting it, no end.
verses.directors_commentary: The vocabulary of numbers returns, with a twist. The stars had a number, which God holds; his understanding has none, so the verse turns the word mispar from a tool of the divine into a measure that fails. 'Our Lord' is adoneinu, the plural of majesty with a suffix, and the 'our' keeps the intimate note: this is not an abstract power. Radak makes a lovely point, that a human king who rules many provinces grows tired and cannot hold both power and wisdom for them all, but this one has both without limit. Tevunah is 'understanding, skill, insight' (the same word used of the craftsman who builds the tabernacle), and the KJV 'infinite' is a reasonable paraphrase for 'no number'. A modern audience might hear this as a bare doxology, but in the Psalter it is a claim aimed at the stars of verse 4: the ones whom Babylon consulted are counted and named, and the Lord's wisdom is not.

philological_notes.note: 'Understanding, discernment, skill'; mind that can distinguish and arrange things. The Hebrew says it has 'no number', not that it is 'infinite' in the abstract sense of the KJV.

verses.translation_literal: Lifting up the humble [is] YHWH, bringing low the wicked to the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD raises the humble, takes them by the arm and sets them on their feet. And the wicked, who held their heads so high? He brings them down, down, until their faces meet the dust.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built as a mirror: one participle lifts, the next lowers, and the LORD stands between them. Both are participles, so this is not a single act in the past but what he is doing, steadily, now. The 'humble' (anavim) are not the meek in temperament. In the Psalms they are the poor and the oppressed, people with no army, no land and no standing in court, and for a people just brought back from exile that is the whole nation. The 'wicked' are those who exploit them. Ibn Ezra reads the two groups as the outcasts of Israel and 'the kings of the nations that were under Israel's hand', so the verse turns the world's order over. Radak is candid that this is not always visible: the wicked sometimes prosper now, and the full reversal belongs to the future.

The KJV 'lifteth up' and 'casteth down' is fair, though 'casteth' adds a hurl that the Hebrew lacks; mashpil is simply 'makes low', the opposite of lifting. 'The meek' is an archaic word for people who today would be called the poor and humble. The verb me'oded is rare and means to raise up, to give support, so the picture is of a hand under the arm. 'To the ground' is literally 'as far as earth', so the wicked go all the way down.

philological_notes.note: A polel participle of the root meaning to surround or return; here it means to support, to hold up, to raise to one's feet. Metzudat Zion glosses it as raising up and strengthening. The participle makes the lifting continuous.
The humble or poor who depend on God because they have no other protection; a social as well as a moral term. Ibn Ezra identifies them with the lowly, the outcasts of Israel.

verses.translation_literal: Answer to YHWH with thanksgiving, make music to our God with a harp.
verses.translation_dramatic: Answer him now. Let the thanksgiving rise from the throat, and let the harp take it up: strings under the hand, a song for the LORD, for our God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist turns from describing God to addressing the congregation, and the command comes as a pair: a verb for the voice, a verb for the instrument. The first verb, ENU, can be read in two ways, and the commentators name both. Ibn Ezra takes it as the poet speaking to Israel, 'answer', as in 'and you shall answer and say'; he also notes others who read it as 'the voice of singing', and the harp is mentioned beside it. Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David read it as raising the voice, citing the Levites who 'answered' in a loud voice at Mount Ebal. The KJV 'sing' follows that second reading, and it is a defensible rendering. If 'answer' is heard, the psalm becomes a response: after hearing what God does for the humble, the people reply.

Todah is thanksgiving, but in the temple it is also the name of a sacrifice and a type of song, so the word has a public, liturgical ring. The harp (kinnor) is the small hand-held lyre of ancient Israel, not the modern concert harp; it was played to accompany praise. Note 'our God': the verse moves from the covenant name to the personal possessive. Malbim sees a distinction here between the LORD as creator of the order of nature and 'our God' who watches over us in particular.

philological_notes.note: Two readings. The root can mean to answer, and Ibn Ezra reads it so ('and you shall answer and say'); it can also mean to raise the voice in song, which is how Ibn Ezra's second group, Metzudat Zion and Metzudat David take it. STEPBible has 'sing'. The literal layer keeps 'answer'.
A hand-held lyre, the instrument of David and of temple praise. It is closer to a lyre than to a modern harp.

verses.translation_literal: The coverer of heavens with clouds, the preparer for the earth of rain, the sprouter on the mountains of grass.
verses.translation_dramatic: He draws clouds over the sky like a cloak. He makes ready the rain for the thirsty earth, and he makes the grass spring up on the hills.
verses.directors_commentary: Three participles with the definite article, each one a step in a chain: clouds, rain, grass. Each is a stage in a single process, so the verse works like a camera tracking from sky to mountaintop. For an audience in the land of Israel, which has no great river to water it (unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia), rain is the whole of life, and it falls only in winter; summer is a long drought. Hence 'prepares': the Hebrew verb is kun, to set up, to establish firmly, as one prepares a place at table. The god of rain in the neighbouring religions was Baal (Hadad), who rode the clouds in the Canaanite myths, and the psalm gives these actions to YHWH alone, in the same way as the contest on Carmel in 1 Kings 18. Radak and Metzudat David point out the mountains: nobody can plough or irrigate there, and so only rain feeds them. The KJV 'maketh grass to grow' is a fair paraphrase of 'causes to sprout'. The word chatzir is fresh grass for fodder, which prepares the animals of verse 9.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle of kun, 'to set firmly, to establish, to make ready'; rain is prepared in advance, like a provision.
Green grass or fodder; the food of the herds, as the next verse shows.

verses.translation_literal: Giver to the beast of its bread, to the sons of the raven who call.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gives the beasts their bread. He feeds even the young ravens when they cry.
verses.directors_commentary: The grass of verse 8 becomes the animals' food, and the verse goes down the scale to the smallest and least loved: the raven, an unclean bird and a scavenger. 'Lechem' is 'bread', which in Hebrew is also a general word for food (Meiri notes that it covers all food, citing Daniel 5:1), so the KJV 'his food' is correct, while the Hebrew gives the animals the same word that people use for their own bread. Livnei 'orev, 'sons of the raven', is a Hebrew idiom for the young of a species. Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David pass on a rabbinic tradition that young ravens are born white, so that their parents think they are not their own and abandon them, and that God then sends insects from their droppings to feed them; that is their natural history, not the psalm's. The idea of God feeding ravens appears also in Job 38:41, and in Elijah's story ravens bring him bread (1 Kings 17:6): the same bird that the law counted unclean serves as a servant of God. The KJV 'which cry' is right; yiqra'u is the same verb as 'calls' in verse 4, so the God who names stars hears the cry of chicks.

philological_notes.note: 'The sons of the raven', the young ravens. Rabbinic comment holds that they are born white and abandoned by their parents; this is tradition, not the text.
Bread, or food in general; Meiri says it stands for all food.

verses.translation_literal: Not in the might of the horse does he delight; not in the legs of the man does he take pleasure.
verses.translation_dramatic: The strength of a war horse does not move him. The swift legs of the runner do not win his delight.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse turns from nature to politics. In the ancient Near East the horse was the weapon of the great powers: chariots and cavalry were the tanks of Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, and Israel's kings were warned not to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). 'Gevurat ha-sus', the might of the horse, is the military power that every neighbour wanted. The second line puts beside it the human equivalent, the legs of the man, the fast runner who carries messages or fights on foot, or flees. The KJV and every English version say 'legs', which is correct: shoq is the lower leg or thigh, and the Hebrew is at once vivid and a little comic, as if God did not care for impressive calves. Rashi reads it as the speed of the runner's legs. Ibn Ezra takes 'the man' to be the rider, while Radak and Metzudat David say it is the person who trusts in horse or flight rather than in God. Two parallel negatives, lo ... lo, fall like blows. The point is made against the stars of verse 4 and the armies of the nations: strength does not buy God's favour.

philological_notes.note: 'The legs of the man': the lower leg or thigh, symbol of a runner's strength and speed, paired with the horse's might as two kinds of military strength.

verses.translation_literal: Taking pleasure [is] YHWH in those who fear him, in those who hope for his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: No, this is what the LORD delights in: those who stand in awe of him, those who wait, with open hands, for his steadfast love.
verses.directors_commentary:
After two negatives in the last verse, the sentence turns on 'but': it is not the horse and not the runner, it is this. The Hebrew opens with the participle roceh, 'taking pleasure', which is the same verb (ratzah) as yirtzeh in verse 10, 'takes pleasure in the legs of a man'. What God does not take pleasure in there, he does here; the KJV has the same English phrase in both verses, but only the Hebrew makes the echo audible in one root. The object is set twice, each with its own 'et', as two descriptions of one people: those who fear him, and those who hope for his chesed.

Chesed is covenant loyalty, which the KJV renders 'mercy'; that is weaker, since it names a bond that carries obligation, not pity. The verb yachal means to wait with expectation, so hoping is a stance of dependence. Radak and Meiri read the two groups as the ones who rely on God and not on the horse or on human strength. Metzudat David adds that whoever trusts in those things removes the fear of the LORD from before his face.

philological_notes.note: The same root as יִרְצֶה in verse 10. The verse answers the previous one: God does not take pleasure in the horse or the runner, but he does take pleasure in those who fear him.
Covenant loyalty: faithful, committed kindness within a bond. 'Mercy' in the KJV narrows it to compassion.
Those who wait in hope. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'those who expect'.

verses.translation_literal: Extol, Jerusalem, YHWH; praise, Zion, your God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Jerusalem, praise the LORD! Zion, praise your God.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now speaks to the city itself, in the feminine singular: Jerusalem and Zion are two names for the same city, addressed as a woman or a mother. The two commands in parallel (shabbechi, halli) are two verbs for praise, the first of which, shabach, means to praise or to calm and is a rarer, more formal word than halal. The second line changes 'YHWH' to 'your God' (elohayikh, with the feminine 'your'), so that the public name gives way to a personal one; Malbim sees in the different names a difference of kind. Zion, strictly the hill with the temple and David's city, and Jerusalem, the whole city, were not separate peoples, as Radak and Metzudat David say: both mean the inhabitants. The KJV 'thy' for the second person singular is archaic but it keeps the singular, which the modern 'you' loses. The city that was rebuilt in verse 2 is now asked to answer: praise is what the rebuilt city gives back.

philological_notes.note: Piel feminine singular imperative of shabach, 'to laud, to extol'; addressed to the city as a woman.
'Your God' with the feminine singular suffix; the KJV 'thy God' keeps the singular that modern 'your' hides.

verses.translation_literal: For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your sons in your midst.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear it, Jerusalem: the bars across your gates are his work, and they hold. And inside, in the middle of you, among the lanes and the courtyards, your sons stand blessed.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene is a walled city at dusk. Bars were heavy beams of wood or bronze slid across the inside of the city gate (Metzudat Zion compares them to a rod laid across the width of the gate to shut it). A city was only as safe as its gates, so a strengthened bar means the one thing that kept the people in and the enemy out will not fail. Play this as relief, not boasting. The speaker is addressing a city that remembers having no walls.

The Hebrew sets two actions in the same tense, strengthening the bars and blessing the sons, and the second sits inside the first: the blessing is 'in your midst', behind the bars. The KJV 'children' is the Hebrew banayikh, literally 'your sons' (the word covers children of both sexes, so 'children' is defensible); the KJV 'within thee' is accurate but flattens 'in your midst', the centre of the city. BBE's 'iron bands' adds a metal the Hebrew does not name.

philological_notes.note: The bar of a gate. It is the same word as for the bars of the tabernacle frames. The verse presents the bar as the visible guarantee of the city's safety.
'In your midst', the middle of the city. It places the blessing inside the protected space.

verses.translation_literal: The one who sets your border [as] peace, the fat of wheat he satisfies you [with].
verses.translation_dramatic: He sets peace along your border like a fence, and the borderlands are quiet. And he fills you, to the full, with the heart of the wheat.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two images of safety, one military and one at the table. The border (gevul) is where ancient cities lost their harvests to raiders, and the grain was the first thing an enemy burned or carried off. Radak and Metzudat David both make this link: peace on the border means the wheat is eaten by those who grew it. Wheat was the prized grain, and the 'fat' of it is the richest part, which Rashi and Radak read as the best and choicest.

The KJV 'He maketh peace in thy borders' is fine in sense, but the Hebrew has no preposition. Peace is the thing placed, 'he sets your border peace', so the border itself is peace. BBE's 'making your stores full of fat grain' gets 'fat' and misses the satisfying: the Hebrew verb is the one for eating until full.

philological_notes.note: 'Fat of wheat', that is the best of it. The same use of chelev as 'the best' appears in Gen 45:18, 'the fat of the land'.
He satisfies you, fills you to the point of fullness; the verb of a meal that leaves nothing wanting.

verses.translation_literal: The one who sends his saying [to] the earth: as far as quickly runs his word.
verses.translation_dramatic: He sends out his saying over the earth, and his word does not walk. It runs, it is already there before the sound has gone cold.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns from the city to the whole earth and from the harvest to what makes the harvest, the weather, and it opens that turn with speech. God's word is a messenger who is sent and who runs. Radak sees a servant running to do his master's will, and reads the word here as the rain that comes at God's say-so.

The Hebrew is compressed. 'Earth' has no preposition, so the saying is sent straight at the earth. The last phrase says 'until swiftly runs his word', which is less a statement of speed than a picture of the word running until it arrives. KJV's 'very swiftly' gets the speed, but the phrase 'ad meherah is a limit, 'as far as quickly'. Ibn Ezra reads the second half as repeating the first. Note the two words for 'word', imrah and davar, set in parallel.

philological_notes.note: A saying, a spoken utterance; the poetic synonym of davar that follows. Radak reads it here as the rain that comes by God's saying.
He or it runs; the word is imagined as a courier on foot.

verses.translation_literal: The one who gives snow like the wool, frost like ashes he scatters.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gives snow, and it comes down soft and heavy as fleece. He shakes out the frost over the ground like ash from a cold hearth.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the first of three winter images, each sharper than the last: snow, frost, ice. Snow like wool is comfort, white and soft, and in a land where snow is rare it is a wonder and a blessing for the soil. Meiri and Metzudat David both note that the comparison is not exact. Wool is less white than snow, and the point is softness and the sense of being covered.

The next image turns. Frost (kefor) falls in the early morning and lies thin on the ground, and its grey colour is that of ash. Radak and Metzudat David say this is why it is likened to ashes rather than to wool. The verb 'scatters' is the one for sowing and spreading, so frost is thrown like seed. The KJV 'hoarfrost' is an old English word for rime; the plain Hebrew is just 'frost'. BBE's 'ice-drops like dust' loses the ash.

philological_notes.note: 'Like ash'. The image is of grey, fine powder on the ground; Radak and Metzudat David explain that frost is likened to ash because it is less white than snow.
Frost, which falls at dawn in the cold season.

verses.translation_literal: The one who throws his ice like crumbs; before his cold, who can stand?
verses.translation_dramatic: He flings his ice down in shards, like broken bread. And before the cold he brings, who can stand?
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes. The soft images are over and the line ends on a question, with a threat in it. Ice is hurled, not given. The verb is the one for throwing something away, a violent verb, and the ice breaks into pieces. 'Crumbs' (pittim) are the bits of a loaf broken by hand; Metzudat Zion links the word to Lev 2:6, 'break it in pieces'. Rashi reads it as ice breaking into small chunks. Say it with the sound of something shattering.

The question 'who can stand?' has no answer, and nobody on stage should give one. The KJV's 'morsels' is correct, and so is its 'who can stand before his cold?'. BBE's 'raindrops' is not in the Hebrew at all. Note that ice here is 'his ice' and 'his cold': Radak stresses that the possessive attributes even the harshest frost to God.

philological_notes.note: 'Like crumbs, like broken pieces'. The root means to break into bits, as with bread (Lev 2:6).
'His cold'. A rare noun for the cold itself.

verses.translation_literal: He sends his word and melts them; he makes his wind blow, [and] waters flow.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then he sends his word again, and it all gives way. He breathes his wind across it, and the water runs.
verses.directors_commentary:
The same word that sent the cold now sends the thaw. This is the hinge of the whole section: the verb 'sends' returns from v. 15 and the 'word' that ran now melts. The ice is no longer a threat, and the line moves quickly, like water beginning to move. Radak understands 'his word' as the sun's heat or rain, and Rashi has the west wind breaking the ice.

The Hebrew word ruach means both 'wind' and 'spirit', and an ancient audience would hear both. The KJV's 'he causeth his wind to blow' is accurate, but it adds the extra clause 'and the waters flow' as though a result, whereas the Hebrew just sets the two side by side: 'he makes his wind blow, waters flow', with no 'and'. Let the second half fall away like a sentence cut short, as water simply runs.

philological_notes.note: 'And he melts them', with the suffix referring back to the snow, frost and ice of vv. 16-17.
He makes blow, causative of nashav. Ibn Ezra distinguishes this heavier stem from the light stem in Isa 40:7.

verses.translation_literal: The one who declares his words to Jacob, his statutes and his judgments to Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: And this same voice that commands the snow speaks to Jacob. It tells Israel its statutes and its judgments.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the weather to the law, with no change of voice. The word that ran across the earth in v. 15 now speaks to one people. Ibn Ezra draws the link directly: statutes and judgments are the reason the rain falls in its season, as in Deut 11:13-14. The listener is meant to hear the same word, now spoken to people.

The verb magid is 'declare, make known'. KJV 'sheweth' is archaic and weaker, since the verb means to tell something aloud to someone, not just display it. Jacob and Israel are one people under two names, a standard poetic pair. 'Statutes' (chukkim) are the fixed decrees and 'judgments' (mishpatim) the rulings; the Hebrew gives both in the plural, which marks a body of law.

philological_notes.note: 'Declares', 'tells'. It is a participle, so this is something he does habitually, not once.
'His statutes and his judgments', a stock pair for the whole body of law. Metzudat David notes that the second line repeats the first.

verses.translation_literal: He has not done so for any nation, and judgments, they have not known them. Praise Yah.
verses.translation_dramatic: He has done this for no other nation. As for his judgments, the others have never known them. Praise the LORD!
verses.directors_commentary:
The last note is both pride and a pause. 'Not so for any nation' makes the gift of the law Israel's alone, and the psalm ends by turning back to praise. Ibn Ezra says it plainly: God gave the Torah only to his own people, set apart as a treasured nation. Radak and Meiri tie it to Deut 4:7-8 ('what great nation has statutes and judgments so righteous?'). Do not play it as contempt for others. The speaker is amazed at a gift, not scorning those who did not receive it.

Two small points. The word 'bal' is a poetic 'not', used here in place of the ordinary 'lo' that opens the line, so the verse has two different words for 'not'. And the closing 'Hallelu-Yah' is two words, 'praise' (plural imperative) and the short form of the divine name. The KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' turns the name into a title; the dramatic layer follows it with 'the LORD' as instructed.

philological_notes.note: A poetic negative, the equivalent of lo. Metzudat Zion says it means the same as 'not'.
'Praise Yah': a plural command to praise, with Yah as the short form of the divine name. It frames the psalm as it opens it.
